1.o: This chapter gives us a more particular account of the beginning of Daniel's life, his original and education, than we have of any other of the prophets. Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, began immediately with divine visions; but Daniel began with the study of human learning, and was afterwards honoured with divine visions; such variety of methods has God taken in training up men for the service of his church. We have here, I. Jehoiakim's first captivity (ver.
1.s: Daniel Asks for Vegetables and Water
1.i: Taken to Babylon, Daniel and his three friends refuse the king's rich food and are blessed by God.
1.p: Lord, give us courage to stand firm in small choices, and wisdom to ask in a kind way. Amen.
1.l: Pick one thing today that is good for you, and choose it instead of something easier.
q: Daniel decided before the test what he would do. What have you decided ahead of time?

2.o: It was said (ch. i. 17) that Daniel had understanding in dreams; and here we have an early and eminent instance of it, which soon made him famous in the court of Babylon, as Joseph by the same means came to be so in the court of Egypt. This chapter is a history, but it is the history of a prophecy, by a dream and the interpretation of it.
2.i: Daniel tells Nebuchadnezzar his dream of a great statue and a stone, and gives God the credit.
2.p: Lord, Your kingdom will never end. Help us to trust that You rule over every power. Amen.
2.l: Look for something in the world that is big and strong today, and remember that God is greater.
q: Daniel said the secret belonged to God, not to him. How do you give God the credit for what you know?

3.o: In the close of the foregoing chapter we left Daniel's companions, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, in honour and power, princes of the provinces, and preferred for their relation to the God of Israel and the interest they had in him. I know not whether I should say. It were well if this honour had all the saints. No, there are many whom it would not be good for; the saints' honour is reserved for another world.
3.i: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue and are thrown into a fiery furnace.
3.p: Lord, You are able to save. Even if the answer is no, help us to stay faithful to You. Amen.
3.l: Remember that God is with you even in hard places, and say, Even if not, I will trust You.
q: The three men said God could save them, but that even if He didn't, they would still be faithful. What does that kind of trust look like?

4.o: The penman of this chapter is Nebuchadnezzar himself: the story here recorded concerning him is given us in his own words, as he himself drew it up and published it; but Daniel, a prophet, by inspiration, inserts it in his history, and so it has become a part of sacred writ and a very memorable part. Nebuchadnezzar was as daring a rival with God Almighty for the sovereignty as perhaps any mortal man ever was; but here he fairly owns himself conquered, and gives it under his hand that the God of Israel is above him.
4.s: The King Who Lived Like an Ox
4.i: Daniel 4 is a king's own letter about the day his pride was broken and his sanity returned.
4.p: Lord, all that we have is Yours. Humble us before our pride breaks us, and let us praise the King of heaven. Amen.
4.l: Practice saying thank you to God today instead of saying look what I did.
q: The king praised God before he went back to business. What do you do first when something is restored to you?

5.o: The destruction of the kingdom of Babylon had been long and often foretold when it was at a distance; in this chapter we have it accomplished, and a prediction of it the very same night that it was accomplished. Belshazzar now reigned in Babylon; some compute he had reigned seventeen years, others but three; we have here the story of his exit and the period of his kingdom.
5.i: At a feast using vessels from the Jerusalem temple, a hand writes on the wall, and Daniel explains that Babylon's time is up.
5.p: Lord, You hold all kingdoms in Your hand. Keep us humble and teach us to learn from others' mistakes. Amen.
5.l: Think about something you treat as small that is really important, and treat it with respect.
q: Belshazzar knew the story of Nebuchadnezzar and did not learn from it. What stories should you learn from?

6.o: Daniel does not give a continued history of the reigns in which he lived, nor of the state-affairs of the kingdoms of Chaldea and Persia, though he was himself a great man in those affairs; for what are those to us? But he selects such particular passages of story as serve for the confirming of our faith in God and the encouraging of our obedience to him, for the things written aforetime were written for our learning.
6.i: Daniel keeps praying despite a law against it, and God shuts the lions' mouths.
6.p: Lord, You shut the mouths of lions. Give us courage to pray and to keep doing what is right. Amen.
6.l: Keep doing what is right today, even if people tell you not to.
q: Daniel's prayer habit was the thing his enemies used against him. What habits of faith do you have?

7.o: The six former chapters of this book were historical; we now enter with fear and trembling upon the six latter, which are prophetical, wherein are many things dark and hard to be understood, which we dare not positively determine the sense of, and yet many things plain and profitable, which I trust God will enable us to make a good use of. In this chapter we have, I. Daniel's vision of the four beasts, ver. 1-8. II. His vision of God's throne of government and judgment, ver. 9-14. III.
7.i: Daniel 7 is the first of Daniel's own visions, and its throne room scene is one of the best-known pictures of God in the Bible.
7.p: Lord, You are the Ancient of Days. Your kingdom will never end. Hold us steady when the beasts roar. Amen.
7.l: When the news seems bad today, remember: God's throne is set, and His kingdom lasts.
q: The saints will share in judging the world through Christ. How does that change how you treat the people you are tempted to write off?

8.o: The visions and prophecies of this chapter look only and entirely at the events that were then shortly to come to pass in the monarchies of Persia and Greece, and seem not to have any further reference at all. Nothing is here said of the Chaldean monarchy, for that was now just at its period; and therefore this chapter is written not in Chaldee, as the six foregoing chapters were, for the benefit of the Chaldeans, but in Hebrew, and so are the rest of the chapters to the end of the book, for the service of the…
8.i: Daniel 8 shifts the book from Aramaic back into Hebrew and gives a vision that history later filled in with surprising accuracy.
8.p: Lord, You know the future. Give us courage to live today with trust, even when we do not see what comes. Amen.
8.l: When you do not understand what is happening around you, say, God is in charge, and go on with your day.
q: Angels desire to look into the great salvation. What about your own salvation have you stopped looking into?

9.o: In this chapter we have, I. Daniel's prayer for the restoration of the Jews who were in captivity, in which he confesses sin, and acknowledges the justice of God in their calamities, but pleads God's promises of mercy which he had yet in store for them, ver. 1-19. II. An immediate answer sent him by an angel to his prayer, in which, 1. He is assured of the speedy release of the Jews out of their captivity, ver. 20-23. And, 2.
9.i: Daniel 9 is one of the great prayers of the Bible, followed by one of its most debated prophecies.
9.p: Lord, hear. Lord, forgive. Lord, listen and act. We trust in Your mercy, not our goodness. Amen.
9.l: Pray today using Daniel's words: We do not ask because we are good, but because You are merciful.
q: A fast was a way to say we are humbled before God. What would that honest confession look like in your own words?

10.o: This chapter and the two next (which conclude this book) make up one entire vision and prophecy, which was communicated to Daniel for the use of the church, not by signs and figures, as before (ch. vii. and viii.), but by express words; and this was about two years after the vision in the foregoing chapter. Daniel prayed daily, but had a vision only now and then. In this chapter we have some things introductory to the prophecy, in the eleventh chapter the particular predictions, and ch. xii. the conclusion of it.
10.s: The Man in Linen by the River
10.i: Daniel 10 to 12 close the book with a heavenly messenger, a long outline of wars between kings, and one of the clearest promises of resurrection in the Old Testament.
10.p: Lord, You know our names and the end of the story. Help us to live in hope, to rest in You, and to rise on the last day. Amen.
10.l: Say thank you to God today that He knows the end of the story, and that you are written in His book.
q: Daniel called the Tigris simply 'the great river.' What is the great river of your daily life that you rarely stop to look at?

11.o: The angel Gabriel, in this chapter, performs his promise made to Daniel in the foregoing chapter, that he would "show him what should befal his people in the latter days," according to that which was "written in the scriptures of truth:" very particularly does he here foretel the succession of the kings of Persia and Grecia, and the affairs of their kingdoms, especially the mischief which Antiochus Epiphanes did in his time to the church, which was foretold before (ch. viii. 11-12). Here is, I.
11.s: The Man in Linen by the River
11.i: Daniel 10 to 12 close the book with a heavenly messenger, a long outline of wars between kings, and one of the clearest promises of resurrection in the Old Testament.

12.o: After the prediction of the troubles of the Jews under Antiochus, prefiguring the troubles of the Christian church under the anti-christian power, we have here, I. Comforts, and very precious ones, prescribed as cordials for the support of God's people in those times of trouble; and they are such as may indifferently serve both for those former times of trouble under Antiochus and those latter which were prefigured by them, ver. 1-4.
